editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech is a diagnosis of deindustrialisation more than a devolution plan. Its evidence is the long shadow of decisions like Ravenscraig's closure. Thirty years on the site is still being filled. Burnham pairs that with today's gaps inside Scotland: one shop in twenty empty in Edinburgh against one in five in Dundee, a seven-year life-expectancy gap across ten miles, and a shrinking working population in Inverclyde.

The remedy offered is mostly administrative: localised employment support, devolved employability and innovation funding, and the 'names not numbers' Easterhouse model scaled up. These may be good ways to run services. But a steelworks was the region's economic base, and redesigning the jobcentre does not replace it. The money named is small next to that hole: £10 million from each government for two defence colleges, and a £1 billion research pot spread across the whole UK. Burnham concedes the point himself when he says 'we can announce all the investment we like'. Better-run local services will matter only if there is new industry for them to connect people to.

The most concrete industrial lever in the speech is not devolution at all but procurement. Burnham chose Falkirk-built buses over the cheapest global bid and now wants all UK public procurement to work that way. That fits a wider pattern in this government: publicly controlled transport used as a buyer of domestic manufacturing, from Greater Manchester's buses to the promised British-built GBR trains. It marks a quiet break with decades of lowest-cost purchasing, and it will face pressure whenever budgets tighten.

There is also a tension in the offer. The powers Burnham proposes to hand to Scottish regions are largely Westminster's own: DWP employment support, innovation and enterprise funding, and research money. Yet his argument is aimed at Holyrood's centralisation. He also warns that Scotland's towns risk being 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up', and says Holyrood's reform timetable is too slow. That sets up a competition in which the UK government can be seen as generous to regions while Edinburgh appears to hold them back. The first test is the National Economic Council meeting he has promised within weeks.

The speech also carries the EU argument into Scotland. Burnham pitches the 20 November food and farming deal as a benefit to Scottish agriculture. His Commons case rested on Scottish salmon checks and banned Scottish seed potatoes. The friction-cost case for a closer European relationship lands hardest in exactly the places where the Union is most contested.
